items.title: Klemperer's LTI
items.claim: Victor Klemperer's LTI: Notizbuch eines Philologen (1947) studied which subject?

options.text: The language of the Third Reich, observed during the war by a Romance philologist who survived persecution

items.reveal_title: A close linguistic analysis of Nazi-era German
items.reveal:
Klemperer (Romanist at Dresden, dismissed in 1935) compiled a study of Nazi-period vocabulary, rhetoric and propaganda forms.

The book has remained continuously in print as a model of linguistic study under dictatorship.
items.why: Documentary records of how a regime uses language can outlast the regime itself.

items.title: East German vocabulary after 1990
items.claim: After German reunification (1990), East German specific vocabulary largely faded. One word that survived in widespread use is:
items.reveal_title: The Ampelmannchen survived as a cultural icon
items.reveal:
Created in 1961 by Karl Peglau, the East Berlin pedestrian-light figure was retained after unification following public campaigns.

Most specifically DDR-era political vocabulary disappeared from active use within a decade.
items.why: Symbols can outlive the political contexts that created them.

items.title: Yiddish speaker numbers
items.claim: Yiddish is a West Germanic language historically spoken by Ashkenazi Jews. About how many speakers worldwide today?
items.reveal_title: Around three quarters of a million today
items.reveal:
Ethnologue and YIVO estimates suggest between roughly 600,000 and 1 million speakers, concentrated in Hasidic communities in the US, Israel, the UK and elsewhere.

Before 1939, estimates suggested over 11 million speakers.
items.why: Catastrophic 20th-century events shaped which Germanic languages survived in numbers.
